thread.title: Google Has Stayed Out of the Hot Seat --- Until Now

author: Barron's
title: Google Has Stayed Out of the Hot Seat --- Until Now
text:
Ramin Talaie/Getty Images For months, some officials at Facebook ( FB ) privately grumbled that the company was taking arrows from lawmakers and regulators over its handling of data while its rivals were largely overlooked.
It was a not-too-subtle jab at Alphabet 's ( GOOGL ) Google, which largely stayed above the fray by remaining silent-to the point of declining to send a top-level executive to last month's Senate Intelligence Committee hearing, which Facebook Chief Operating Officer Sheryl Sandberg and Twitter Chief Executive Jack Dorsey both attended. An empty chair at the hearing representing Google said it all.
Now it's Google's turn in the hot seat.
Late Monday, Google shuttered its Google+ social network following the disclosure that personal data for hundreds of thousands of users was potentially exposed because of a bug it kept quiet. The bug, which was fixed in March, potentially impacted as many as 500,000 Google+ users, though the data was limited to optional profile fields such as a person's name, email address, gender, and age, according to Google.
"Given these challenges and the very low usage of the consumer version of Google+, we decided to sunset the consumer version of Google+," the company said in a statement .
Alphabet stock was down slightly, to $1,151.76 per share, in afternoon trading on Tuesday. But for the year, stock in Google's parent company is up 10%. That's compared to a 10% drop for Facebook, which has been the piñata over concerns about data and privacy on social media. Tim Cook, the CEO of Apple ( AAPL ), has been a vocal-and frequent- critic of Facebook and Google but few have focused on Google.
Until recently.
Google Chief Executive Sundar Pichai is scheduled to visit the White House next week as part of a gathering of "big internet companies, big social-media companies, search companies," White House chief economic adviser Larry Kudlow said last week. "And some who are dissatisfied with those companies."
Google's handling of the situation is bound to make things more complicated for Pichai at a time when Facebook is taking renewed heat for another breach that may have affected at least 50 million accounts, according to computer-security experts.
"What's most concerning here is that Google did not feel the need to disclose the breach, and today's privacy laws don't require it," Theresa Payton, a former Chief Information Officer at the White House and Chief Executive of security firm Fortalice, tells Barron's .
"People ask me what keeps me up at night," Payton says. "One of the many things that worries me is the overall privacy and security of the platforms that know us the best, the ones we use every day. In this case, instead of Facebook, it's Google that had a long standing open issue."
For the most part, Google has adroitly avoided the political spotlight. But its disclosure about Google+ and its decision to drop out of bidding for a 10-year, $10 billion cloud-computing contract for the Pentagon amid employee backlash has changed the calculus significantly. Google said the contract, in part, could have conflicted with its corporate values governing artificial intelligence.
